claude.sample_unit: data points (images, patches, reviews, clinical note samples)

links.outcome: Model performance differences by skin tone (Fitzpatrick I-II vs V-VI) on dermatology images
links.effect: Ground-truth NPV was 0.83 vs 0.78 for skin tones I-II vs V-VI; SUDO AUC 0.60 vs 0.58, both indicating bias favouring I-II.
links.quote: Our findings demonstrate that both SUDO and the traditional approach (with ground-truth labels) identified a bias in favour of patients with a Fitzpatrick scale of I-II, which is consistent with previously-reported bias findings 14 .

links.outcome: Subgroup performance gap by skin tone on Stanford DDI hidden without subgroup evaluation
links.effect: NPV 0.83 (Fitzpatrick I-II) vs 0.78 (V-VI); SUDO AUC 0.60 vs 0.58, showing a bias in favour of lighter skin tones.
links.quote: This discrepancy, calculated without ground-truth labels, is indicative of the bias we also observed when using ground-truth labels and the negative predictive value of the predictions (NPV) (NPV = 0.83 and 0.78, respectively).

links.outcome: Performance degradation of dermatology models under distribution shift to a new deployment dataset
links.effect: DeepDerm and HAM10000 AUC fell from 0.88 and 0.92 on development data to 0.56 and 0.67 on Stanford DDI data.
links.quote: We purposefully chose two AI models (DeepDerm 15 and HAM10000 16 ) that were performant on their respective data (AUC = 0.88 and 0.92) and whose performance degraded drastically when deployed on the DDI data (AUC = 0.56 and 0.67), suggesting the presence of distribution shift.

links.outcome: Performance of models on withheld versus in-the-wild data with distribution shift
links.effect: Dermatology models performing well on withheld data (AUC 0.88, 0.92) dropped to AUC 0.56 and 0.67 on the external DDI dataset.
links.quote: We purposefully chose two AI models (DeepDerm 15 and HAM10000 16 ) that were performant on their respective data (AUC = 0.88 and 0.92) and whose performance degraded drastically when deployed on the DDI data (AUC = 0.56 and 0.67), suggesting the presence of distribution shift.

Flagging low-reliability predictions for human expert review

links.outcome: AUC after deployment on shifted DDI images
links.effect: DeepDerm/HAM10000 AUC fell from 0.88/0.92 to 0.56/0.67 on DDI.
links.quote: We purposefully chose two AI models (DeepDerm 15 and HAM10000 16 ) that were performant on their respective data (AUC = 0.88 and 0.92) and whose performance degraded drastically when deployed on the DDI data (AUC = 0.56 and 0.67), suggesting the presence of distribution shift.

links.outcome: Model selection agreement with ground-truth AUC
links.effect: SUDO ranked HAM10000 above DeepDerm: AURCC 0.86 vs 0.62; ground-truth AUC 0.67 vs 0.56.
links.quote: Specifically, HAM10000 and DeepDerm achieve an area under the reliability-completeness curve of AURCC = 0.86 and 0.62, respectively and, with ground-truth annotations, these models achieve (AUC = 0.67 and 0.56).

links.effect: Fitzpatrick I-II vs V-VI: SUDO AUC 0.60 vs 0.58; NPV 0.83 vs 0.78; bias favored I-II.
links.quote: Our findings demonstrate that both SUDO and the traditional approach (with ground-truth labels) identified a bias in favour of patients with a Fitzpatrick scale of I-II, which is consistent with previously-reported bias findings 14 .

links.effect: Despite prior AUC 0.88/0.92, models achieved DDI AUC 0.56/0.67 under distribution shift.
links.quote: We purposefully chose two AI models (DeepDerm 15 and HAM10000 16 ) that were performant on their respective data (AUC = 0.88 and 0.92) and whose performance degraded drastically when deployed on the DDI data (AUC = 0.56 and 0.67), suggesting the presence of distribution shift.
